title: Web Application Structure
keywords: separating routing, application services, and data access
subtopics: Separating routing, application services, and data access.
learning_outcomes: Explain what web application structure contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: front-controller architecture.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: A web request carries a method, path, headers, and optional data; PHP uses these to produce a status, headers, and body. Keep HTTP details separate from application rules and templates. In this lesson, focus on front-controller architecture; then compare it with controllers and handlers. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use web application structure when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A web request carries a method, path, headers, and optional data; PHP uses these to produce a status, headers, and body. Keep HTTP details separate from application rules and templates. For web application structure, begin with front-controller architecture. Also distinguish controllers and handlers; views and templates; shared layout files. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
